solution: Parallel planes \(\Rightarrow\) normals proportional: \((2,-\lambda,1)\parallel(4,-1,\mu)\). \(4 = 2 \cdot 2\), so \((4,-1,\mu) = 2(2,-\lambda,1)\): \(-1 = -2\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac12\) and \(\mu = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\). Thus \(\left(\frac12,2\right)\).
note: The line mixed two scale factors (1/2 and 2) and trailed off; with (4, -1, mu) = 2(2, -lambda, 1) it gives lambda = 1/2, mu = 2 cleanly.

solution:
Let \(Q(2\lambda-1,\ 3\lambda+2,\ 6\lambda-3)\) be a point on the line which is at 3 unit distance from the point \(A(-1,2,-3)\). \(\therefore AQ=3\)
\(\therefore \sqrt{(2\lambda)^2+(3\lambda)^2+(6\lambda)^2}=3\ \therefore (2\lambda)^2+(3\lambda)^2+(6\lambda)^2=9\ \therefore 49\lambda^2=9\)
\(\therefore \lambda=-\frac{3}{7}\ or\ \frac{3}{7}\)
\(\therefore\) There are two points on the line which are at a distance of 3 units from A.
Their co-ordinates are \(Q(2\lambda-1,\ 3\lambda+2,\ 6\lambda-3)\).
Hence, the required points are \(\left(-\frac{1}{7},\ 3\frac{2}{7},\ -\frac{3}{7}\right)\) and \(\left(-1\frac{6}{7},\ \frac{5}{7},\ -5\frac{4}{7}\right)\).
note: The base point is A(-1, 2, -3); there is no P.

solution:
A plane making equal intercepts \(a\) on all three axes has intercept equation
\(\dfrac{x}{a}+\dfrac{y}{a}+\dfrac{z}{a}=1\ \Rightarrow\ x+y+z=a\)
It passes through \(A(1,2,3)\): \(1+2+3=a\Rightarrow a=6\).
It passes through \(B(3,2,1)\): \(3+2+1=a\Rightarrow a=6\).
Both points give the same value \(a=6\), so the plane is
\(x+y+z=6\)
The vector equation is
\(\therefore \bar{r}\cdot\left(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}\right)=6\).
(Note: with the equal-intercept condition \(x+y+z=a\), both given points force \(a=6\), so it is the only such plane with non-zero intercepts.)

The stem asks for plane(s): besides the nonzero-intercept plane above, the degenerate case of equal (all-zero) intercepts is a plane through the origin. The plane through the origin containing \(A(1,2,3)\) and \(B(3,2,1)\) has normal \(\overline{OA}\times\overline{OB}=(1,2,3)\times(3,2,1)=(-4,8,-4)\propto(1,-2,1)\), giving
\(x-2y+z=0\), i.e. \(\bar{r}\cdot(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=0\)
(check: \(A: 1-4+3=0\), \(B: 3-4+1=0\)). So the two required planes are \(x+y+z=6\) and \(x-2y+z=0\).
note: The note said 'unique' while the answer gives two planes; x - 2y + z = 0 has all intercepts 0.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key \(\lambda=-\dfrac{10}{11}\) does not make the lines perpendicular; the correct value is \(\lambda=\dfrac{70}{11}\), which zeros the sum of products of direction ratios.]

Reduce each line to symmetric form to read direction ratios.
Line 1: \(\frac{1-x}{3}=\frac{x-1}{-3}\); \(\frac{7y-14}{2\lambda}=\frac{y-2}{2\lambda/7}\); \(\frac{z-3}{2}\). Direction ratios: \(-3,\ \frac{2\lambda}{7},\ 2\).
Line 2: \(\frac{7-7x}{3\lambda}=\frac{x-1}{-3\lambda/7}\); \(\frac{y-5}{1}\); \(\frac{6-z}{5}=\frac{z-6}{-5}\). Direction ratios: \(-\frac{3\lambda}{7},\ 1,\ -5\).
Lines are perpendicular \(\Rightarrow\) sum of products of direction ratios \(=0\):
\((-3)\left(-\frac{3\lambda}{7}\right)+\frac{2\lambda}{7}(1)+(2)(-5)=0\)
\(\frac{9\lambda}{7}+\frac{2\lambda}{7}-10=0\Rightarrow\frac{11\lambda}{7}=10\)
\(\therefore \lambda=\frac{70}{11}\).
